EntertainmentTab.title: Jeff Bezos was 'heavily involved' in Robert Pattinson's casting as Bond
EntertainmentTab.text:
Jeff Bezos has said he was "heavily involved" in casting Robert Pattinson as the new James Bond.

Speaking at an event in California, the Amazon chairman said he was originally "biased against" Pattinson - who starred in many blockbuster films like Batman and the Twilight series - "because he's already so famous".

The role of 007 has typically gone to an actor who is not as well known at the time of casting. But Bezos said in screen tests, "it was so obvious he is James Bond".

This will be the first 007 film in the official series not under the creative control of the Broccoli family, who had overseen the franchise since the first movie in 1962. Amazon purchased MGM, which co-owns the franchise, in 2022.

"There was something special about Rob", Bezos said at Semafor Silicon Valley & The World Event on Tuesday.

Pattinson was unveiled as the franchise's seventh James Bond on Monday, taking over from actor Daniel Craig. He will star in the 26th Bond movie, due to be released in 2028.

In a statement, the London-born actor said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime."

The next Bond film will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, but its title and exact release date have not yet been announced.

The announcement comes after years of intense speculation about who will take over from Craig in one of the most high-profile - and highly scrutinised - roles in entertainment.

Several other actors, including Josh O'Connor, Callum Turner and Jack Lowden, were reported to be in the frame for the role as screen tests took place in recent weeks.

But Amazon MGM ultimately went with a household name, choosing a more bankable movie star who is widely seen as a safe pair of hands.

"We ran a really tight process and made the final decision on Friday," Bezos said.

There were five finalists who went through "real, old-fashioned screen tests", acting out three different scenes in full costume, with real sets and other actors, he said.

"By the time we got to this list of five, they were all amazing. But there was something special about Rob and his performance," Bezos added. "It was immediately un-debated. Denis [Villeneuve], the director … we all gravitated toward Rob."

The pick comes amid widespread Hollywood cuts and consolidation, with studios struggling to get people into cinemas.

Hollywood insiders have said Pattinson was viewed as a safe pick to bring audiences in, rather than taking a risk on a new actor who could grow with the franchise.

"Maybe he's boring. Maybe Hollywood would be passing up a chance to anoint a badly needed new star. But with so much at stake for everyone involved, that all makes him the obvious pick," Hollywood journalist Matthew Belloni, who predicted the pick, wrote in his newsletter.

The BBC's Regan Morris contributed to this report.

EntertainmentTab.title: Hunger Games prequel Sunrise on the Reaping splits opinion: 'Surreally awful' or 'surprisingly strong'
EntertainmentTab.text:
Reviews of the latest Hunger Games film have seen it dismissed as a "surreally awful prequel" and "a tortuous, costly mess" by some critics - but called "surprisingly strong" and "one of the best films in the series" by others.

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth movie in the franchise, and tells the origin story of a teenage Haymitch Abernathy - who was played as an adult by Woody Harrelson.

In a one-star review, the Guardian called the film, external "overwrought and boring", and said it "has no actual interest and no authentic reason to exist, other than to gouge an income stream out of its fanbase".

But the Wrap praised its, external "memorable performances, intoxicating style and horrifying commentary", adding: "When the dust settles it may even be the Hunger Games that holds up best."

Sunrise on the Reaping is set 24 years before the first Hunger Games film, and 40 years after the previous prequel, 2023's The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.

"This prequel lands at some mid-point between Ballad and Hunger Games, which puts it on an immediately odd footing," Empire said in a three-star review, external.

"It can't escape the sense of feeling supplementary. It's an enjoyable-enough diversion, but essentially a footnote with aspirations."

Screen Daily called it, external an "underwhelming prequel", which "suffers from a lack of compelling characters" and "feels oddly incidental - a drab afterthought rather than a crucial new chapter".

EntertainmentTab.title: Ex-rugby player Danika Priim says sex assault 'never happened'
EntertainmentTab.text:
A former England rugby league player and TV pundit accused of putting her hand up a woman's skirt in a cricket club toilet has told a jury it "categorically did not happen".

Danika Priim, 42, has been charged with carrying out the alleged sexual assault in the toilets at Horsforth Cricket Club in Leeds on 22 July 2022.

Her accuser, who cannot be named for legal reasons, previously told a trial at Leeds Crown Court how Priim twice reached up her dress and grabbed her underwear.

Keighley-based Priim, who previously represented Bradford Bulls, Leeds Rhinos and England, including at the 2017 World Cup, denies one count of sexual assault. The trial continues.

Two of the complainant's friends told the court they also witnessed what happened in the toilet but, on Wednesday, Priim told the jury she was never in the toilets with the three women.

Prosecutor Chloe Hudson put it to Priim that there were only two alternatives – either she was lying or the complainant and her two friends were lying.

Priim told the jury: "It categorically did not happen."

The defendant agreed she was not suggesting that it was an accident, or the woman had invited her to touch her, or it was a joke.

Priim told the jury she was never in the toilets with the complainant, adding: "I did not touch (her) in the toilets at all."

Hudson said to her: "What you must be saying is that these three got together to make completely false allegations about you."

Priim responded: "It's the biggest question I have – it's the why."

The prosecutor asked the defendant about how the complainant demonstrated to the jury how she was grabbed.

Priim said: "She was lying. I did not do that."

She added: "I'm also a very happy heterosexual woman. I'm with a man. I live with a man."

The prosecutor said: "The truth is that you sexually assaulted (the woman), didn't you?"

Priim said: "The truth is that it never happened."

EntertainmentTab.title: Channel 4 admits it doesn't know number of Married At First Sight UK sex abuse complaints
EntertainmentTab.text:
Channel 4's chief executive has admitted she doesn't know how many complaints of sexual misconduct were received about Married at First Sight UK, despite a six-month external review into the hit TV show.

When asked by MPs, Priya Dogra said: "I'm not sure I have the details," adding that the review looked specifically at the claims of three women featured in a BBC Panorama.

Married at First Sight UK was cancelled after Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members, while a third woman alleged a non-consensual sex act. The men involved have denied all the allegations.

Separately, Dogra said the broadcaster "cannot apologise enough" to a former employee who twice made complaints about Russell Brand and felt they weren't properly handled.

Dogra said it was "almost unforgivable" that the woman said she complained to Channel 4 in 2009 and again in 2023.

Brand is serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after recently being found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Married at First Sight UK, known as MAFS UK, had been running for 10 seasons and was one of Channel 4's biggest shows, with audience figures often topping three million.

The Panorama investigation in May heard from three women who made allegations about the men they were partnered with - claims the men deny:

One woman said her on-screen husband raped her and threatened her with an acid attack.

A second woman told both Channel 4 and production company CPL, before broadcast, about being allegedly raped by her on-screen husband. Her episodes were still aired.

A third woman accused her on-screen husband of sexual misconduct.

All three women accused the show of not doing enough to protect them.

A review was commissioned into MAFS UK by Channel 4 shortly after the BBC first contacted the broadcaster with details of the allegations.

Earlier this month, the completed review recommended extra safeguards on the show. But Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation.

Speaking to MPs on the House of Commons culture and media committee on Tuesday, Dogra was repeatedly asked if she knew how many allegations Channel 4 and CPL had received over the years that MAFS UK was on air.

"I looked specifically into those instances [the three women], I did not do a broad sweep of every episode or every season of the show. That is not what the terms of reference for the show were," she responded.

"If there are others, we would take them seriously and look into them on the same basis."

Channel 4's bosses were also questioned at length about Brand by MPs in the hearing.

Brand's work on Channel 4 included hosting Big Brother sister show Big Brother's Big Mouth and its celebrity equivalent from 2004 to 2007, a chat show in 2006, and appearing on Big Fat Quiz of the Year.

Addressing Dogra and Channel 4's chairman Geoff Cooper, MPs said the member of staff who made two complaints about Brand "fell through the cracks".

In response, Dogra said: "I'm not sure we can apologise enough as an organisation for putting her through that twice. We have apologised in public in the past and in private."

She accepted that the woman's complaints were "not handled properly" and added that "it's almost unforgivable that happened twice".

When asked by the committee if junior members of staff could raise complaints against a star without fear of losing their job, Dogra replied she "can't say 100%" that that would be the case.

"What I can do is set the standard, set the tone, make sure that the facilities are available, make sure that my staff and the production companies understand the repercussions of not complying, and understand the kind of culture that I'm trying to set, and we're trying to set as an industry."

She also said she found the "cultural personality" around Brand "horrendous".

"I find it distasteful, and I look at the jokes... that is the lowest form of humour, because these are jokes that are made at the expense of someone else's physical safety.

"I don't believe it should have been acceptable then, and I certainly don't think it's acceptable now."

During the session, Dame Caroline also put to Channel 4 bosses that in both the MAFS UK and Brand cases, the broadcaster appeared like "a child with their hand in the cookie jar".

The committee chairwoman asked: "To what extent can you reassure us that Channel 4's priority is genuinely the welfare of the staff who work there, the staff who have worked there, and the people who take part in your shows - rather than purely when the world is looking at you and you suddenly feel that you've got a reputational reason to take a look at these shows?"

Dogra responded by saying that when Channel 4 commissioned the review, "we didn't even know whether the Panorama programme would be made".

She added: "We had received a right-to-reply letter and the programme came out six weeks later, but it equally it could not have been made. We always intended to do the review."

In the instance of the woman who tried to complain about Brand, she added: "I'm not sure there are more apologies we can give. Because none of those things should've happened."

If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.uk

EntertainmentTab.title: Birmingham university pauses Shakespeare Institute move after backlash
EntertainmentTab.text:
The University of Birmingham has paused plans to move the Shakespeare Institute from Stratford-upon-Avon to Birmingham amid growing opposition to the proposal.

The university said it would spend the next six months working with partners including the Royal Shakespeare Company (RSC) and the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust to explore the institute's future in Stratford.

The decision comes after criticism from Stratford-upon-Avon MP Manuela Perteghella and a petition that attracted more than 12,000 signatures.

The move from its home at Mason Croft had been due to take place in September.

The postgraduate research institute announced on Friday that it had been told it would leave Stratford and relocate to the University of Birmingham's Edgbaston campus, with future plans unclear for its Mason Croft base, historic gardens and playing fields.

Announcing the pause on Tuesday evening, University of Birmingham vice-chancellor and principal Prof Adam Tickell said he had heard "very clearly" how much the institute mattered to Stratford-upon-Avon and the wider Shakespeare community.

"I have therefore decided to pause the planned move as we explore how and whether the Institute can have a vibrant and viable future in Stratford-upon-Avon," he said.

EntertainmentTab.title: Tricks! Traps! Riddles! Jan van Eyck’s portraits look vividly real – but are full of secret messages. What do they mean?
EntertainmentTab.text:
At the Barbican Art Gallery in London, there is an exhibition of some of the white paintings made by the US artist Robert Ryman over 60 years from the 1950s. The paintings are square, because a square is neutral, and he didn’t want viewers associating them with the visual language of landscape or portrait. For Ryman, his paintings resolutely were what they were, which is to say, white paint applied to various surfaces and fixed to the wall. Not “windows” through which one could glimpse another world.

At the National Gallery, a couple of miles across town, is an exhibition of 10 works by the 15th-century Flemish painter Jan van Eyck. With one exception – the Arnolfini portrait, which is a one-off in all kinds of ways – they are all A4-size portraits, each angled so that we see more of the left than the right side of their faces. Aside from the likenesses of the people who paid for them in some of his religious paintings, including the Ghent altarpiece, these are the sum total of Van Eyck’s surviving portraits.

In a manner profoundly different from Ryman’s works, Van Eyck’s portraits pull you from our world into his. The precision of his physiognomies is dizzying. In his portrait of his wife, Margaret, recently conserved and on loan from Bruges, she regards you with a steady gaze, her lips firm and decisive. Between her cheek and ear is a blemish, a slight discolouring of the skin; her left eyebrow is bisected by a scar. Her headdress contains seven layers of frothing lace that you want to pinch between your thumb and finger. What must it have been like, to look back at this vision of yourself, in a world in which mirrors were luxury items (and mostly convex, like the one that famously hangs at the back of the Arnolfini portrait)?

We know it’s her, because a very detailed inscription in the painter’s hand on the original frame tells us that “my husband Jan completed me on 15 June 1439” and that “my age is 33 years”. By some stroke of painterly enchantment, is it Margaret herself addressing us? Or is the “me” the painting – a mere arrangement of oil paint on a panel of Baltic oak? The inscription concludes with the words “as I can” – Van Eyck’s motto, a phrase that hovers between extreme modesty and great boastfulness.

All the portraits have something of this uncanny hyper-realistic quality. The pockmark on the slightly shiny, reddish young skin. The lines around the eyes and crinkled cheeks of the old scholar in his red robe, and his ear, purplish with age. The scar between the eyes of the stubbled Baudouin de Lannoy, who worked alongside Van Eyck at the court of Philip the Good, the Burgundian ruler of the Low Countries. The individual hairs of a fur collar as they brush the skin of the neck; the intricate whorls of an ear. You feel that if these people reached out their beringed fingers and tugged you through the frame, you could walk about with them, in the streets of Ghent or Bruges of the 1430s.

Perhaps the most arresting of these faces is the portrait of Jan de Leeuw, who, like Margaret, gazes straight at the viewer. He has such a modern-seeming face that it’s hard to shake the impression that he might have sat beside you on the morning commute. Like Margaret, he has his original frame, around which Van Eyck has painted words that translate as: “Jan de Leeuw who, on Saint Ursula’s day, opened his eyes for the first time, 1401. Jan Van Eyck has counterfeited me. It can be seen when he began 1436.” Beautiful precision, all the more satisfying because the Van Leeuw in question can be found in Bruges’ city archives: from a family of goldsmiths, he was himself the inspector of the goldsmiths’ guild at the time of the portrait. Everything checks out: he’s holding a gold ring.

Except that it doesn’t. Like all the works in the exhibition, its apparent “truthfulness” turns out to be a trap, its mirror-like reality a game of illusion and deceit. “He counterfeited me” – the word is “gheconterfeit” – is such a strange word to use, especially of a man who assessed the quality of gold. In its 15th-century context, it was an ambiguous word, says show’s co-curator Nicholas Flory, also “used in documents to describe a true likeness or reliable copy of a real thing”.

But Van Eyck is also deeply unreliable. The painted words are a trompe l’oeil, convincing you they are inscribed in brass. The man’s name, which means “lion”, actually appears as a cute pictogram, as a little joke. To add to the confounding, certain letters of the inscription are made to look as if they are standing out in relief. If you take these and treat them as Roman numerals, they add up to the dates crucial for the painting: 1401 and 1436. In other words, the portrait, which at first seduces with its “reality”, turns out on second glance to be a highly artificial, self-conscious construct. The paint counterfeits metal for its goldsmith sitter, and sets puzzles for the viewer. The ring De Leeuw is holding is so terribly real – and also, so desperately fake.

The Arnolfini portrait is another example of apparent clarity melting swiftly away to complete bafflement. It is one of the best known works in the National Gallery, so familiar to British art lovers that it is possible to forget how strange it is. For centuries, this image of a man taking hold of a woman’s hand was known as the “Arnolfini marriage”, because it was assumed to commemorate an actual wedding ceremony. In the 1930s, Erwin Panofsky posited that every item in the busy domestic interior (the oranges, the wooden overshoes, the mirror, the dog, the burning candle and the guttering candle in the beautifully painted chandelier) was weighted with matrimonial symbolism.

But in truth, no one even knows for sure whether it represents members of the mercantile Arnolfini family (the identification was made based on 16th-century inventories in which the picture said to portray “Hernoul le fin” or “Arnoult Fin”, which were thought to be corruptions of the name Arnolfini). And more recently, many critics have pulled back to accept a more straightforwardly materialist interpretation of the scene: the oranges, the ridiculously voluminous green dress, the fine furnishings, are all markers of status, rather than symbolic as such.

As for the inscription – it reads: “Johannes de eyck fuit hic [was here] 1434”. Again, it seems so clear – but where on earth is “here”? Does it mean Van Eyck was witness to some actual event that he depicted? Or that he painted himself as one of those figures dimly visible in the convex mirror? Or that the main figure is actually a self-portrait, and that this pale man with the large hat and flared nostrils – also the subject of a second portrait in the show – is Van Eyck himself? The inscription breaks the fourth wall: it seems to be hovering on the picture plane itself. So is “here” the metaphysical “here” of the artist’s imagination?

There is one certain self-portrait of Van Eyck, and that, characteristically, is another trick. It is not in this exhibition, but rather in a religious work in the Groeningemuseum in Bruges, the Virgin and Child With Canon Joris Van der Paele. Van Eyck hid in his painting in a tiny image of himself – identifiable by his paintbrush – reflected in the metal shield of Saint George. The ageing canon has removed his spectacles, perhaps the better to appreciate the supernatural vision of the Virgin and child.

The National Gallery’s show opens with a work from its own collection that is frequently regarded as a self-portrait. The realist details are bewitching, intimate: the bloodshot red eyes, the fine lines around them, the stubbled cheeks, the exuberantly painted red hat. On its original frame is painted a signature (“Jan van Eyck made me on 21 October 1433”) along with the motto “as I can” – the position of which, where one would often find the name of the sitter, helps build the case that the work depicts the painter himself. Here, the writing appears to be deeply incised into the surface, playfully implying that the frame is of solid gold, rather than the gilt that it really is.

The more you crane and gaze at these paintings, admiring the wrinkles and the spots and the all-too human flesh, the more you trip up on Van Eyck’s tricksiness. The slippage between being fooled by the illusion and recognising that you are being fooled is part of the pleasure. The more you look, the more you feel you’re having a conversation with the painter – and that he is having the last laugh.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘Most extraordinary virtual world’: critics hail Grand Theft Auto VI as masterpiece
EntertainmentTab.text:
Good things clearly come to those who wait. After 13 years of anticipation, Grand Theft Auto VI is finally here – and, according to critics, it’s a masterpiece.

The trailer for the video game, which returns players to Vice City, Rockstar’s fictional version of Miami, attracted more than 90m views in 24 hours when it was released in December 2023. Excitement continued to mount, with two release delays and a steady stream of leaks and speculation keeping the game in the headlines.

Now, Metacritic, which aggregates reviews from critics, averages it at 99 out of 100 – tying with Nintendo’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, which has held the record for the best reviewed video game since 1998.

In a five-star review, the Guardian’s Keza MacDonald said: “In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen.”

MacDonald praised the fictional state of Leonida as an extraordinarily detailed world, populated by incidental encounters and activities that make it feel alive. But for all its violence and grotesque humour, what stood out was the relationship between Jason and Lucia – GTA’s first female protagonist.

She said: “I was rooting so hard for Jason and Lucia by the end that I felt quite sick with worry about what was going to happen to them, pacing back and forth in front of my TV throughout the final missions. Among all the expectations I had for GTA VI, I did not expect it to make me so emotional.”

In a 10-out-of-10 review, IGN’s Luke Reilly called it “the single most impressive video game I have ever played”. He praised its graphics, driving mechanics and the sheer amount of detail in its world.

He said: “I see no real limit to the amount of time I could spend here, endlessly exploring and interacting with Vice City and the massive area surrounding it. While the well-paced story effectively nudged me around the map, there are still vast sections of it that I’m yet to even visit – despite hitting the credits after almost 120 hours of hijinks.

“Frankly, I’ve never played anything that’s hit quite like GTA 6 – and right now I have zero plans to stop playing it.”

In its five-star review, Eurogamer said Rockstar had “pushed back the horizon of video games once again” with its graphics, storytelling and world building.

Chris Tapsell wrote: “It’s about big ideas, themes, places – America, society, love – and also about individuals. It’s ridiculous and puerile, and also sometimes mature. Tender and violent. Deep and shallow. Novel and, in places, surprisingly familiar.”

For the New York Times, the game was “about love and relationships, their joy and heartache, and the work required to make them successful”.

Yussef Cole’s review said this reflected a maturation of a series that had “generally only told stories about men solipsistically chasing after their own success”. Whether you’re controlling Jason or Lucia, he added that “much of what you can do – apart from activities routine to GTA like stealing cars and robbing banks – is taking action to care for and nurture your romantic partner”.

The Washington Post’s Gene Park awarded the game four stars, saying it “raises the bar at every level”. He highlighted its unusually convincing portrayal of human behaviour, with more than 33,000 individual non-playable characters and interactions shaped by race, class, gender and money.

Writing for Forbes, Paul Tassi singled out the relationship between Jason and Lucia as one of the game’s greatest achievements, saying: “I can’t say I’ve ever seen a better video game relationship than the one they share.”

Bloomberg’s Jason Schreier gave the game five stars, calling it a “masterpiece”. “It’s hard not to be astonished by what Rockstar has done here. There’s nothing else like it,” he said.

GamesRadar+ also awarded it full marks, calling it “the ultimate time vampire”, and VGC suggested its influence will be felt across the games industry for years to come. Reviewer Jordan Middler described Rockstar as operating at “the absolute peak of its power”, adding that GTA 6 was “one of the best video games ever made”.

Grand Theft Auto VI officially launches on Thursday. Rockstar has not revealed the cost of the game, but some estimates put the figure north of $1bn (£760m).

In the UK, the standard edition costs £69.99, rising to £89.99 for the Ultimate Edition. The research firm Sensor Tower estimated that the game had generated $1.54bn (£1.2bn) in digital pre-orders by 17 November, while analysts have forecast that it could generate between $3.25bn and $5.2bn in sales during its first week.

GeneralTab.title: China's Xi Jinping has orchestrated a remarkable diplomatic moment
GeneralTab.text:
Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.

For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.

Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.

And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.

Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.

His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.

But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.

First, China is not keen for the war in Ukraine, now well into its fifth year, to be on the agenda.

This is a delicate balancing act for Xi who is aware his relationship with Putin may damage China's connections in Europe. The EU is a key market, especially now when the Chinese economy is heavily relying on exports.

However Xi also doesn't want the war to end in a way that will destabilise Russia, a key ally and neighbour.

Beijing is still trying to maintain that it is neutral in this war and has repeatedly called for negotiations and a political settlement while avoiding condemnation of Russia's full-scale invasion.

Donald Trump has already made it clear he wants the three leaders to discuss limiting the world's supply of nuclear weapons.

The US and Russia possess the world's largest stockpile of nuclear warheads. But China is rapidly expanding its own arsenal, which is raising alarm bells in Washington.

The last major US-Russian arms control treaty, known as New START, expired in February this year, triggering fears of an arms race. The agreement had set a cap to control the number of nuclear weapons in US and Russia's arsenal.

Trump would like China to be included in any new agreement, but Beijing has pushed back.

Xi's argument will be that his arsenal is considerably smaller than what Washington and Moscow own, and, therefore, it would be unfair for Beijing to be bound by their limits. China also believes it should have the freedom to develop its own nuclear capabilities.

He may hope to use this as propaganda at home, given the country is grappling with huge domestic challenges.

A country-wide property crisis has dented consumer confidence. Local governments are heavily in debt. Manufacturing has slowed and more of China's workforce has become dependent on flexible jobs with no pension or social security. One in five young people are thought to be struggling to find work. Frustration and anxiety about the future bubble up routinely.

Xi does not have to deal with elections, and the country has not seen major protests in decades. But he will be concerned about his popularity within the party elite as these problems - and the palpable frustrations they produce - grow.

At a time like this, a photo-op with Putin and Trump may offer him proof that his country's "century of humiliation" is over. China is no longer a rising power, he can argue - rather, it is increasingly shaping the rules of a new era.

GeneralTab.title: McDonald's sex abuse: 'They were waiting for the younger girls to turn 18'
GeneralTab.text:
A former McDonald's worker who says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers, has called on the firm to “change the way they treat younger employees”.

Hope, who worked at a branch in the West Midlands in 2023, also told BBC News she saw older colleagues eyeing up 16- and 17-year-old workers, and talking about wanting to sleep with them when they turned 18.

Hope is one of hundreds of workers bringing a discrimination claim against McDonald's. This week, a judge ruled against McDonald's attempt to have their claims struck out, a move that Hope welcomed.

McDonald's said: "Ensuring a safe, respectful and inclusive working environment across our restaurants and offices remains a fundamental priority."

The latest developments come after a BBC investigation in 2023 which heard that workers, some as young as 17, were being groped and harassed.

Last year, McDonald's staff told us they still faced sexual abuse and harassment.

Hope, who is now 22, says that her branch of McDonalds had a very sexualised, "toxic" environment.

She spoke of a time a manager came up behind her and put his hands on her shoulders. From then on, whenever she saw him coming over, she says she "moved quick" to get away from him.

"I got the hell out of there," she says.

Another time, she says a manager failed to protect her when she says she was being sexualised and objectified by two customers on a night shift.

Hope says she told the manager what was happening, but he told her to "just suck it up and deal with it".

Her main concern, however, was for the younger teenagers, who she says weren't being looked after.

"You could tell there were other staff members waiting for their 18th birthdays. That sort of like toxic culture where it's like, 'Oh, you know, it's not illegal now.' It was that feeling from quite a few of them," she says.

"And why would you? That is literally a child still."

Hundreds of current and former McDonald's employees are bringing a discrimination claim against the firm.

The fast-food chain had attempted to have the complaints thrown out but this week at the London Central Employment Tribunal, Judge Glennie ruled that 450 cases can go ahead and they are now expected to be heard at the Employment Tribunal in April.

The BBC understands that these relate to indirect discrimination, not sexual harassment.

Hope told us she was not taking part in the legal case for money, saying they didn't know if they were going to get anything.

Instead, she said it was to try and "change the way they treat younger employees".

"It's going to change the way they treat allegations. It's going to shake up the whole internal process and make life easier for the kids who are now having their first jobs. And it's going to make it a lot safer, I think, as well. And that's something you can't put a price on, the safety of the young these days.''

She also accused McDonald's of trying to "delay the inevitable" by attempting to have the claims thrown out.

"And the judge quite rightly looked at them and said: 'No. We're not going to do that.'"

GeneralTab.title: 'Feudal' leasehold system set to be scrapped in England and Wales
GeneralTab.text:
The government is to introduce new laws to scrap the way flats are built in England and Wales.

Under the proposed bill, most new leasehold flats will be banned and replaced with commonhold, where residents collectively own and manage their buildings.

Matthew Pennycook, the housing minister, said the current leasehold system was "blighting lives" and was an "anachronism in the twenty-first century".

The legislation follows Labour's 2024 election manifesto to "bring the feudal leasehold system to an end" - with further details expected to be set out later.

However, freeholders argue the policy is "unjust" and will have a detrimental impact on investment markets.

The proposed Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill will also include capping ground rent - the annual fee paid by current leaseholders to their freeholder - at £250. That will then be reduced to a "peppercorn" rate - which is effectively nothing - after 40 years.

Fozia Malik lives in a one-bedroom flat in Oldham and says her ground rent will go up from £150 to £300 in January. That is alongside service charges of more than £4,000 a year.

Malik says her block of flats has been plagued by a number of problems, including fire safety issues and rising costs.

The managing agent for her building says the service charges are due to costs that are out of its control and high insurance because of fire safety issues.

But Malik says she would "never" buy a leasehold flat again, describing it as a "continuous torture cell".

When she bought her flat, Malik assumed the system would work in the same way it does in Pakistan, where she grew up, and in most other countries, where buying a home also means owning a share of the land it sits on.

However, in England, most flats are sold on a leasehold basis. That gives the buyer the right to occupy and use a property for a set period of time, but the freeholder retains ultimate ownership of the building and the land.

Systems based on shared ownership and collective management - such as commonhold - are already standard in many parts of the world, including Australia, New Zealand, the US, Canada and much of continental Europe. They give residents ownership of their home and a stake in the building's common areas.

The government says its reforms are intended to bring England and Wales more closely in line with other international models.

It comes as more than 1,000 leaseholders have contacted the BBC over the past two years with complaints about the current system.

GeneralTab.title: AI giant Anthropic valued at up to $1.5tn ahead of stock market debut
GeneralTab.text:
Anthropic has seen its value jump to as much as $1.5tn (£1.14tn) as its shares are set to start trading on the stock market on Thursday.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said its shares will be priced at $83 each when it lists on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.

That will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

Anthropic's stock market debut will make it the first US firm focused exclusively on AI to go public. It will also mark a crucial test for the fast-growing industry, which faces questions over whether the huge amounts of money being poured into the technology will be profitable.

The firm said earlier this month it would offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn.

But demand for Anthropic's stock debut - commonly referred to as its initial public offering, or IPO - is very high, according to one early investor in the company who spoke with the BBC on condition of anonymity.

The person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of the public listing, meaning demand for Anthropic shares exceeded the number of shares available.

If that turns out to be the case, Anthropic's valuation could quickly blow past its target on Thursday when trading begins.

Depending on how strong that demand is, Anthropic could even exceed the early market valuation of Elon Musk's SpaceX, which was the world's most highly valued stock debut when it went public with a value of $2.2tn in June.

However, in the weeks that followed, SpaceX shares fell significantly in price.

As it stands, Anthropic's listing will see the firm raise more than $68bn from its initial investors. It is also expecting another $26bn from private placements. So the total amount the company will raise is expected to be $94bn.

The amount of cash Anthropic has raised from its listing is already more than SpaceX raised in June.

OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT and Anthropic's biggest AI rival, is expected to go public next year.

Until then, Anthropic will be the only public company in the US that is entirely focused on the technology, or one that was founded and built around AI tools and products. Its scope is different from tech giants like Google and Microsoft that also develop AI but are involved in other tech services.

There is excitement around Anthropic's listing, but also some concern from investors around its ability to generate revenue and profits going forward.

Yang Wang, a principle financial analyst with Counterpoint Research, said the central issue for Anthropic is whether its business "can keep pace" as hundreds of billions of dollars in financial obligations come due in the next couple of years.

"Nevertheless, it is not an everyday occurrence for public investors to gain direct exposure to a frontier-model developer with the potential to shape the next stage of productivity," Wang said.

While nearly every other major tech company is pouring huge amounts of money into the technology and infrastructure required for their own AI tools, they are built around social media or online retail or online search. AI tools and applications are secondary.

"Anthropic going public gives us a whole new window into what AI demand looks like," Marta Norton, who heads strategy at investment firm Empower, told the BBC.

Norton said Anthropic going public now, in a time of market volatility comes down to the simple fact that the company needs access to more money.

"AI is financially demanding," Norton said. "The public markets open up the financial spigot a little bit more, and so the time has come."

But broader anxieties have started to grow about the AI industry's business model, which is reliant on expensive computer chips that are in short supply. The technology is also dependent on controversial data centres and funding such operations require deals with other tech companies.

The Federal Reserve Bank has expressed concern about the rapid growth of AI-related debt being financed through "complex and opaque" structures, according to minutes from its October meeting to discuss a potential rate rise.

A few of the meeting's participants also noted that "AI-related exposures were becoming increasingly concentrated among a small number of firms".

With additional reporting by Rachel Clun

GeneralTab.title: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
GeneralTab.text:
It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.

Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.

But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.

So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer."

The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival – Anthropic.

Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.

It is about to sell shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.

The sale comes at a crucial time when many are wondering whether, amid increasing concern about the potential of AI, the industry's bubble is showing signs of bursting.

Where once investors were "all in" on a technological revolution to rival the railroads, the car, electricity and the internet, some are now hedging their bets, amid arguments that AI prices will be driven down as the technology becomes more common and concerns that a hefty wedge of the AI investment is tech giants investing in each other.

Shares in companies that supply the raw computing power behind AI, like Coreweave and Nebius, have seen their value cut in half while even the mighty Nvidia has lost its crown as the world's most valuable company with its shares down 30% - a staggering $2tn fall in value.

So could the Anthropic IPO reinflate the bubble or will it be remembered as the last gasp of a boom that is heading for a bust?

At an event last week, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei told JPMorgan Chase's CEO Jamie Dimon that his guiding principle was to "never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it's worth".

The company is selling roughly $65bn worth of shares to the general public and a further $26bn on to other big tech companies. It is comfortably the single biggest money raising event in US corporate history.

It's an old adage that during a gold rush you should buy companies that sell the picks and shovels as opposed to those staking everything on striking gold. In AI's case that's the chip makers, the data centre builders, the energy providers. But Anthropic is arguably the gold itself and this IPO will see what value people put on it, according to Fiona Cincotta.

"I think the reason that this IPO is so important is basically it's the first ability for the public investors to access a pure play AI trade," she says, adding that previous offerings have been about "other parts of the ecosystem, which are, the semiconductors, the chips, the, data centres. But this is the first time that we were actually able to access the AI provider."

What a company is worth depends almost entirely on predicted future earnings.

It's that calculation that many think presents the sharpest needle to the AI bubble.

Will current and future users of AI be prepared to pay enough to justify the trillions being spent on the chips, data centres, energy and employees, some of whom can command annual salaries of over $100m?

"AI is certainly in a financial bubble. While LLMs [large language models] offer genuine utility and are undoubtedly here to stay, the economics don't add up," said Gary Marcus, Professor Emeritus at New York University and author of Taming Silicon Valley, speaking earlier this year.

"[The] more companies build AI models, the [more the] technology becomes commoditised, eliminating meaningful competitive advantages and driving down prices."

So far, the growth rates in Anthropic revenue are extraordinary.

It's not just some Wall Street investors questioning whether the AI boom is all it's cracked up to be. Out on Main Street, ordinary Americans have concerns too.

With the US driving so much of global AI growth, a growing public backlash against a technology that threatens to replace millions of jobs and hoover up vast amounts of energy and water became a factor in the recent midterm elections in the US.

Many areas in the US have passed moratoriums on data centre development and many candidates deemed too close to big tech found that association a political liability rather than an asset. Many Democrat candidates publicly opposed data centre development and won.

Added to that, the Pied Piper of AI, chip maker Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang, resigned last week after admitting to having been "unfaithful" to his wife after reports he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang.

Huang's spectacular fall from grace and Nvidia's 30% fall in value from its peak have left AI investors looking for a new champion for the AI boom that has underpinned the US stock market and arguably much of its entire economy for the last two years.

If Anthropic – and its CEO are to be AI's new Pied Piper, he will be playing a different tune to the relentlessly upbeat, leather jacket-clad talisman Huang.

While Huang wanted AI development to continue full throttle, Anthropic was built on misgivings over the levels of safety and responsibility the OpenAI leavers felt were being exercised over the development of society-changing technology.

Amodei has warned that AI capabilities could enable biological weapon development, mass surveillance, authoritarianism and the replacement of millions of white-collar, tax-paying workers.

He has called for a slowdown in its development as its powers are growing at such an exponential rate that it could very soon elude any human oversight.

That said, his paternalistic overtures have been sceptically received by those who point out that the pace of Anthropic's development of new more powerful models has shown no sign of the slowdown he's advocating for the rest of the industry.

But for all the concerns, just as with Elon Musk's SpaceX before it – the hype and the FOMO (fear of missing out) on an undoubtedly profound moment in technological and perhaps human development – means that buying interest is high.

It's reported that orders to buy shares exceed the number on offer by over six times.

With demand outstripping supply by such a margin, a first-day jump is likely given the oversubscription, but it doesn't tell you much about long-run return.

Using SpaceX as an example again, shares initially rose nearly 70% from its IPO sale price of $135 to $225. Shares in SpaceX are currently back to $145.

The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful and blow a bit of fresh new air into what some maintain still looks a lot like a bubble.

Eileen Burbidge, founder of tech investors Passion Capital, is one of those who reject the notion that AI is a bubble about to burst.

"Maybe the growth of the bubble has slowed down a little bit, but actually I wouldn't be willing to say that it's about to burst yet," says Burbidge. "I think this IPO could actually mean everyone could be off to the races again."

Fiona Cincotta believes Anthropic's IPO is about far more than just Anthropic. "I think what's going to be really interesting here is I think it can actually be used as a valuation benchmark for the entire AI ecosystem," she says.

"That's why I don't think this is just going to affect the share price of Anthropic. I think this is going to have much wider implications across the whole AI trade."

Two things can be true at the same time. The Anthropic IPO could be wildly successful - FOMO is a powerful emotion in financial markets. But its probable success won't soothe the unease in some quarters that not every company, every investor and every citizen will think of AI as the answer to humanity's problems.

Xi does not have to deal with elections, and the country has not seen major protests in decades. But he will be concerned about his popularity within the party elite as these problems - and the palpable frustrations they produce - grow.

At a time like this, a photo-op with Putin and Trump may offer him proof that his country's "century of humiliation" is over. China is no longer a rising power, he can argue - rather, it is increasingly shaping the rules of a new era.

articles.title: McDonald's sex abuse: 'They were waiting for the younger girls to turn 18'
articles.text:
A former McDonald's worker who says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers, has called on the firm to “change the way they treat younger employees”.

Hope, who worked at a branch in the West Midlands in 2023, also told BBC News she saw older colleagues eyeing up 16- and 17-year-old workers, and talking about wanting to sleep with them when they turned 18.

Hope is one of hundreds of workers bringing a discrimination claim against McDonald's. This week, a judge ruled against McDonald's attempt to have their claims struck out, a move that Hope welcomed.

McDonald's said: "Ensuring a safe, respectful and inclusive working environment across our restaurants and offices remains a fundamental priority."

The latest developments come after a BBC investigation in 2023 which heard that workers, some as young as 17, were being groped and harassed.

Last year, McDonald's staff told us they still faced sexual abuse and harassment.

Hope, who is now 22, says that her branch of McDonalds had a very sexualised, "toxic" environment.

She spoke of a time a manager came up behind her and put his hands on her shoulders. From then on, whenever she saw him coming over, she says she "moved quick" to get away from him.

"I got the hell out of there," she says.

Another time, she says a manager failed to protect her when she says she was being sexualised and objectified by two customers on a night shift.

Hope says she told the manager what was happening, but he told her to "just suck it up and deal with it".

Her main concern, however, was for the younger teenagers, who she says weren't being looked after.

"You could tell there were other staff members waiting for their 18th birthdays. That sort of like toxic culture where it's like, 'Oh, you know, it's not illegal now.' It was that feeling from quite a few of them," she says.

"And why would you? That is literally a child still."

Hundreds of current and former McDonald's employees are bringing a discrimination claim against the firm.

The fast-food chain had attempted to have the complaints thrown out but this week at the London Central Employment Tribunal, Judge Glennie ruled that 450 cases can go ahead and they are now expected to be heard at the Employment Tribunal in April.

The BBC understands that these relate to indirect discrimination, not sexual harassment.

Hope told us she was not taking part in the legal case for money, saying they didn't know if they were going to get anything.

Instead, she said it was to try and "change the way they treat younger employees".

"It's going to change the way they treat allegations. It's going to shake up the whole internal process and make life easier for the kids who are now having their first jobs. And it's going to make it a lot safer, I think, as well. And that's something you can't put a price on, the safety of the young these days.''

She also accused McDonald's of trying to "delay the inevitable" by attempting to have the claims thrown out.

"And the judge quite rightly looked at them and said: 'No. We're not going to do that.'"

articles.title: 'Feudal' leasehold system set to be scrapped in England and Wales
articles.text:
The government is to introduce new laws to scrap the way flats are built in England and Wales.

Under the proposed bill, most new leasehold flats will be banned and replaced with commonhold, where residents collectively own and manage their buildings.

Matthew Pennycook, the housing minister, said the current leasehold system was "blighting lives" and was an "anachronism in the twenty-first century".

The legislation follows Labour's 2024 election manifesto to "bring the feudal leasehold system to an end" - with further details expected to be set out later.

However, freeholders argue the policy is "unjust" and will have a detrimental impact on investment markets.

The proposed Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill will also include capping ground rent - the annual fee paid by current leaseholders to their freeholder - at £250. That will then be reduced to a "peppercorn" rate - which is effectively nothing - after 40 years.

Fozia Malik lives in a one-bedroom flat in Oldham and says her ground rent will go up from £150 to £300 in January. That is alongside service charges of more than £4,000 a year.

Malik says her block of flats has been plagued by a number of problems, including fire safety issues and rising costs.

The managing agent for her building says the service charges are due to costs that are out of its control and high insurance because of fire safety issues.

But Malik says she would "never" buy a leasehold flat again, describing it as a "continuous torture cell".

When she bought her flat, Malik assumed the system would work in the same way it does in Pakistan, where she grew up, and in most other countries, where buying a home also means owning a share of the land it sits on.

However, in England, most flats are sold on a leasehold basis. That gives the buyer the right to occupy and use a property for a set period of time, but the freeholder retains ultimate ownership of the building and the land.

Systems based on shared ownership and collective management - such as commonhold - are already standard in many parts of the world, including Australia, New Zealand, the US, Canada and much of continental Europe. They give residents ownership of their home and a stake in the building's common areas.

The government says its reforms are intended to bring England and Wales more closely in line with other international models.

It comes as more than 1,000 leaseholders have contacted the BBC over the past two years with complaints about the current system.

articles.title: Van Gogh painting sells for $190.4m after row over Nazi history
articles.text:
Auction house Sotheby's has sold a painting by Vincent van Gogh for a record $190.4m (£144.8m).

The sale of Châtaigniers en fleurs ("Chestnut Trees in Blossom") shatters the renowned artist's previous auction record of $117.2 million set in 2022.

The historic sale in New York on Wednesday comes after an eleventh-hour agreement was reached to resolve a dispute regarding claims the art piece was previously sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

Châtaigniers en fleurs was painted in 1890 in the final two months of Van Gogh's life. It is considered one of the most important works of art from that period to remain in private hands, according to Sotheby's.

It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.

The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.

Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

"In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.

Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.

It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.

The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.

Four other owners then had the painting.

The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

articles.title: Prince Harry, after Ukraine trip, warns on threat from Russia
articles.text:
The Duke of Sussex, who carried out a surprise visit to Ukraine at the weekend, has said he would rejoin the military if asked, as he warned of the threat from Russia.

He told the Telegraph, external he thought people were right to be nervous in the current international political climate and said it was time to "double our support" for Ukraine.

There appeared to be warnings about President Trump - with Prince Harry saying there was a big separation between what the American public thinks about Ukraine and the administration's attitude.

Prince Harry, able to speak more freely than working royals, said he hoped after the US mid-term elections it would be "fantastic to have more American support" for Ukraine.

Speaking to the Telegraph's Dominic Nicholls, Prince Harry said he thought the threat to Europe had been there for the past 15 years - and he felt like it had been at war for the past decade.

"Just because there's not drones, bullets, and rockets flying at us, it doesn't mean that we're not at war," said Prince Harry.

Prince Harry had been in Lviv in Ukraine on Saturday and Sunday - and had told the BBC and journalists at events that he thought the "rest of the world will continue to support" Ukraine.

He had told his Ukrainian hosts, about a conflict with Russia that has already lasted more than four years: "You're going to win the war."

In his Telegraph podcast, he called for a similar unity that was being shown by Ukraine, and feared that Europe could be divided and could "turn on itself".

He addressed the shifting position of US President Trump in a way that is unusual for a royal.

"I think there's been a big separation between what American society feels regarding support for Ukraine, which I think is incredibly high and always has been, compared to a certain group, or in, in this case, an administration that was perhaps thinking about it differently," said Prince Harry.

"As of January, things are going to change, so I think we should all be looking forward to that," he said, referring to the US mid-term elections, which saw significant setbacks for President Trump.

The BBC has approached the White House for comment.

Having served in the military in Afghanistan, Harry said he would return if needed for a future conflict: "If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel."

Prince Harry had received an enthusiastic welcome when he visited Lviv in Ukraine at the weekend, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games.

There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women, some of the 150,000 seriously wounded war veterans in the country.

His visit had been carried out with a press blackout for security reasons - and the night before journalists arrived in the city to cover the visit, there had been air raid warnings that had forced Prince Harry's planning team to head for the shelters.

"Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," Prince Harry had said, including inventing new ways of treating the growing number of injured casualties.

"War is a terrible thing," he said in Lviv, but hailed the resilience of the Ukrainians who had been badly wounded in their defence against Russia's invasion.

articles.title: Myanmar faces historic genocide verdict at UN court over Rohingya massacres
articles.text:
When the judges of the International Court of Justice read out their verdict in the seven-year-old genocide case filed by The Gambia against Myanmar on Thursday, they could make history.

In the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948, after the Nazi Holocaust, dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for the crime of genocide, in conflicts such as those in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.

But no state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.

"It would be a judgment of landmark importance if The Gambia were to win this case," says Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar at the court. "It would give renewed vitality to the 1948 Genocide Convention and to the notion of international legal accountability for crimes committed by a state."

The mass expulsion of the Rohingya population of Rakhine State in August and September 2017 was without question a military operation of exceptional brutality.

I was among a very small number of journalists who witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages in Rakhine, and also the dreadful human suffering of the hundreds of thousands who fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.

Their accounts of killing, torture and mass rape by Burmese soldiers have been thoroughly documented by human rights groups and a United Nations fact-finding mission, external.

I have on many occasions interviewed ethnic Rakhine people about their animosity towards the Muslim population, and I have documented the systematic obliteration of what remained of Rohingya villages by the Myanmar state.

But the question posed at the UN's top court, the ICJ, is whether all of this amounted to genocide.

The ICJ was established in 1945 to help settle disputes between states, not to try international crimes. However, it was chosen to address the attacks on Rohingyas in Myanmar because there were few other avenues of redress for the victims.

Myanmar authorities have denied accusations of ethnic cleansing or genocide, saying they were only responding to terrorist actions by Rohingya militants with so-called military "clearance operations".

A UN report in 2018, based on hundreds of interviews, said the army's tactics were "grossly disproportionate to actual security threats". It said top military figures in Myanmar must be investigated for genocide in Rakhine State and crimes against humanity in other areas. Myanmar rejected the report.

As Myanmar was not a signatory to the International Criminal Court, it was not possible to file a case there against the officials accused of atrocities in Rakhine State.

Instead in November 2019 The Gambia, backed by the Organisation of Islamic Co-operation, filed a case at the ICJ, arguing that all states are bound by the Genocide Convention, so all have an interest in upholding it.

It accused the state in Myanmar, not just the military, of genocide.

This was a novelty in international law; a state not directly affected by an act, arguing that it had legal standing to make a complaint because it was indirectly affected by any violations of such an important convention.

Myanmar objected to this argument, but the ICJ judges ruled that The Gambia was eligible to file the case.

The case drew even more attention when the Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, who at the time headed the elected government in Myanmar, chose to lead the initial legal defence of her country at The Hague in person, for which she was widely criticised.

She had very limited influence over the actions of the Myanmar military in Rakhine State, but her refusal to condemn them dismayed many of those who until then had admired her courage and adherence to democratic principles.

Since she was deposed by a coup in 2021 and placed under arrest the defence has been led by a new team appointed by the military.

Historically, proving that genocide has been committed has been very difficult. Judges apply a high bar to this.

Typically, where there is no explicitly genocidal programme, like that of the Nazis, the judges require that the evidence presented at court must be such that the only reasonable inference from the actions of the defendants is that they had genocidal intent.

When Bosnia-Herzegovina filed a genocide case against Serbia at the ICJ in 1993, it took the court 14 years to conclude that while incidents like the 1995 massacre at Srebrenica did amount to genocide, there was not sufficient proof that the state of Serbia had genocidal intent, though it was found to have failed to prevent genocide.

Myanmar's lawyers and Aung San Suu Kyi have argued something similar.

Suu Kyi said that The Gambia's team mischaracterised a complex conflict and military operation, and that while she accepted that war crimes may have been committed against the Rohingyas, that is not proof of genocidal intent.

But for the huge Rohingya diaspora this verdict matters a great deal.

"This is like formal recognition of our suffering," says Mohammed Nowkim, a Rohingya who was driven out of the Rakhine town of Buthidaung in 2017 and now lives in Canada.

"For the Rohingya, this trial is a moment of acknowledgement of our suffering after years of denial. The Rohingya have been waiting for justice for decades, not just this year."

He and other Rohingya activists hope that a ruling in favour of The Gambia will prompt more co-ordinated action by other countries to find a resolution which allows them to go home to Rakhine State, in safety.

More than a million are stuck in wretched camps in Bangladesh, barred from employment as international funding dries up.

But the obstacles to realising this hope are formidable.

Rakhine State has been ravaged by a conflict between the military and the insurgent Arakan Army, which now controls most of the territory. It is supported by the indigenous Rakhine population who are very hostile to the idea of the Rohingyas coming back.

Many Rohingya villages have been completely destroyed. And international support for them has faded over the years. Even an unprecedented genocide verdict at the world's highest court cannot change that reality.

articles.title: Why children lie and it is important they do
articles.text:
When drawings appear on the wall or biscuits disappear from the tin, your child might blame the dog or claim there was a ghost - even if they are clutching crayons or covered in crumbs.

Children telling fibs is something most parents experience, but such dishonesty and deception is an important part of mental development.

"It's actually a skill that they're developing and that they will play with in order to get better," clinical psychologist Dr Jade Redfern tells the CBeebies Parenting Download podcast.

Here, experts explain why learning to lie is a sign of healthy behaviour - and how to help encourage honesty.

Young children aren't quite sophisticated enough to lie, says Redfern, but they are capable of deception before the age of one.

One of the studies mentioned on the podcast comes from the University of Bristol, external, which found that around a quarter of children appear to understand some form of deception by the time they are ten months old.

Prof Elena Hoicka, who led the study, says it was fascinating to see how "surprisingly young" kids could be so adept and cunning, including her own.

"As a mother of three, I can certainly vouch for how artful and wily they can be.

"Hiding under the table or in the bathroom to eat sweets or chocolate is their common ploy."

Hoicka says that the kind of deception a child uses from the age of two is quite basic - like pretending not to hear their parent or denying they've done something.

"It could also extend to doing forbidden activities in secret," she says. "For example, looking in a bag they were told not to look in when no one is apparently watching, or making excuses, such as claiming to need the toilet when asked to tidy up."

By the age of three, they have become much more proficient and creative in their deceptions, showing a deeper understanding of language and how other people's minds work.

She says they also start to withhold information. For instance, truthfully telling their parents that their sibling has hit them but omitting the fact that they hit their sibling first.

These deceptions are a sign of them developing something Redfern calls "theory of mind".

"As children grow up, we want them to learn and develop the skill that they are their own human being with a separate mind and intentions," she explains.

"This is how [they] develop the skills in empathy, or being able to think about another person's thoughts and feelings that might differ from their own."

Another reason a child might lie is self-preservation as they don't want to upset or disappoint their parent.

"All human beings are driven by attachment," says Redfern. "[Children are] driven by being able to preserve that relationship with their caregivers as they depend upon it."

Early on, they learn what brings them closer to their caregiver and what pulls them apart, she says. With this in mind, Redfern thinks you can encourage honesty by creating a safe environment for a child to tell the truth.

"[We] have to think about ways we can help children feel safe enough to tell us the truth [when] they've made a mistake... and they don't want to disappoint us."

This is something Rachel Duffy, who won the latest series of The Traitors, tells the CBeebies Parenting podcast the she has been trying to do.

The mum-of-three recalls one occasion when her eldest son borrowed his brother's bike and broke it after crashing it into a car. Initially, he tried to lie about what happened.

"I said to him, 'You'll not get into big trouble when you tell me the truth.' I just left and gave him a little space.

"And he went, 'Yeah, that was me.' And then he knew that space was safe. We had a conversation - no raised voices, no roaring or shouting."

Redfern says this is a good example of how to deal with such a situation and that there are occasions when a lie, or nuance, might be appropriate - such as when they receive a gift they don't want or describe other people physically.

"My kids delightfully told me recently that I was very wrinkly," she says. "Again, I try to take it with open curiosity."

She does this by talking about why they think she is wrinkly.

"I think just being able to explore as children get older, just having open, curious conversations - it really develops empathy for somebody else's feelings when they've been shown and modelled empathy over and over again."

articles.title: Putin's Crimean Bridge comes under attack again, Russian official says
articles.text:
The Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, a Russian official has said.

The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea.

The critical bridge had already been hit twice earlier in the week resulting in severe damage and part of the bridge collapsing into the water.

The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.

It comes as Russian President Vladimir Putin meets US President Donald Trump and China's President Xi Jinping on Thursday for landmark talks in China.

Aksyonov confirmed the strike on the bridge in the early hours of Thursday via Telegram, adding that assessment of the damage was under way.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian sources have continued to issue air raid alert warnings overnight for districts just outside of the capital Kyiv.

At least four people were killed in a Russian drone attack on the southern city of Odesa on Wednesday, according to Odesa Governor Oleh Kiper. Officials described the attack as "brutal and deliberate... directly targeting people and their lives".

President Volodymyr Zelensky called the initial strikes on the Crimean Bridge an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

articles.title: Israeli military launches rare ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
articles.text:
Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents.

Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes.

The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.

The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.

Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.

Early on Wednesday afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the incursion and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety.

It also said a section of the north to south Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.

Later, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had begun a joint operation with the Shin Bet security service "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".

"IDF troops under the Southern Command are deployed in the area in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and will continue to operate to remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts by the Hamas terrorist organisation to harm Israeli civilians or IDF troops, or to violate the agreement," it added.

Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".

Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the announcement.

In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man can be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he says.

Automatic gunfire can be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.

A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."

"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."

A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".

Asked about reported fatalities, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.

articles.title: Parents jailed for torture and death of four-year-old girl in France nearly 40 years ago
articles.text:
The mother of a four-year-old girl killed in central France and found along a motorway almost 40 years ago has been sentenced to 20 years in prison.

Halima El Bakhti, 72, was found guilty on Tuesday of "torture and acts of barbarity resulting in death without the intent to kill", French media reports.

The girl's father, 74-year-old Ahmed Touloub, was handed a 15-year sentence as an accomplice.

Four-year-old Inass Touloub was found along the A10 road in Suèvres in the Loir-et-Cher department on 11 August 1987. Her body bore multiple marks of abuse, including human bite marks, broken bones and burns with an iron.

She was buried in an unmarked grave near the location where her body was found. Unidentified for three decades, she was known only as the "Little Martyr of the A10".

Then, in 2018, she was identified after the DNA of her brother – tested in an unrelated case – matched with hers, leading to the arrest of their parents.

The trial took place in Loir-et-Cher Assize Court from 2 November, with the verdict delivered on Tuesday after several hours of deliberation.

During the trial, prosecutor Anaïs Allio emphasised that "not a single part of Inass's body was spared", and recalled the "sense of vertigo that overcame us all" upon viewing the "unbearable photographs" from the autopsy, France Info reports.

The jury concluded that the child's mother was suffering from impaired judgement at the time of the girl's death, which reduced the maximum potential sentence.

French media outlet France Info described the two defendants as sitting stoically in chairs before the court with their heads bowed as the reasoning behind the verdict was read out.

El Bakhti and Touloub have 10 days to appeal the verdict.

Inass's death sparked one of France's biggest ever investigations, with the girl's photograph posted in public places and an alert sent to more than 30 countries.
